These are thin British-style pancakes, and they suit a low sodium diet because they contain no added salt. They take about 20 minutes and make around 8 pancakes.

Ingredients:

- 100 g plain flour
- 2 medium eggs
- 300 ml semi-skimmed milk
- 15 ml sunflower oil, plus a little extra for frying
- Unsalted butter for the pan, about 10 g

Method:

Sift the flour into a large bowl. Make a well in the centre and crack in the eggs. Whisk the eggs gently while drawing in the flour from the edges.

Pour in the milk a little at a time. Keep whisking until the batter is smooth and has the thickness of single cream. Stir in the 15 ml of oil and leave the batter to rest for 10 minutes.

Heat a non-stick frying pan over a medium heat. Add a small knob of unsalted butter and let it melt. Pour in about 50 ml of batter and tilt the pan so it spreads thinly.

Cook for about one minute until the edges lift and the underside turns golden. Flip the pancake with a spatula and cook the other side for 30 seconds. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding a little butter to the pan as needed.

For toppings, fresh berries, sliced banana and a squeeze of lemon juice all work well. A drizzle of honey adds sweetness without adding any sodium worth noting.

The printing press, introduced to Europe by Johannes Gutenberg around 1450, transformed how information moved across the continent. Books that once took months to copy by hand could now be produced in large numbers. Prices fell, and written knowledge reached far more people.

Literacy and learning spread as a result. Merchants, craftsmen and townspeople began to buy books for themselves. Universities and scholars gained access to standard texts, which reduced the errors that creep in through hand copying.

Religion was reshaped as well. Martin Luther's writings spread rapidly in the early 1500s, carried by cheap pamphlets. The Reformation might have stayed a local dispute without print. Instead it became a continental upheaval that split Western Christianity.

Science benefited too. Researchers could share findings, diagrams and data in identical form. Works such as those of Copernicus and Vesalius circulated widely and invited scrutiny. Knowledge became cumulative, with each generation building on printed work.

Language and identity changed over time. Printers favoured particular dialects, which helped standardise spelling and grammar. National languages grew stronger, and shared reading fostered a sense of common culture.

Political authority was challenged by the new medium. Rulers and the Church tried to control what was printed through censorship and licensing. These efforts were never fully successful, and ideas travelled across borders despite them.

Computers slow down mainly because their software grows heavier while their hardware stays the same. Each update to the operating system and to applications adds features. Those features demand more processing power and more memory than the original machine was built to supply.

Storage wear plays a large part too. A hard disk drive (HDD) loses speed as files scatter across its platters. A solid-state drive (SSD) slows as its memory cells wear and its free space shrinks. Either way, the machine takes longer to load programs and open files.

Background processes pile up over time. Many programs install helpers that launch at startup and keep running unseen. Together they consume memory and processor time, so the computer has less capacity left for the task you actually want to do.

Dust and ageing thermal paste cause a separate problem. Clogged fans and dried paste stop the processor from shedding heat efficiently. The chip then reduces its own speed to protect itself, a behaviour called thermal throttling.

Malware and clutter add further drag. Unwanted programs, browser extensions and adverts steal resources quietly. A full disk also leaves the system little room for temporary files.

Most of these problems have fixes. Uninstalling unused programs, clearing startup items, cleaning the fans and upgrading to an SSD or adding memory can restore much of the original speed. A fresh installation of the operating system often helps most of all.

A river carves a canyon mainly by cutting downward into its bed. Moving water carries sand, gravel, and larger rocks. These particles scrape against the bedrock like sandpaper, and the process is called abrasion. Over thousands of years, the grinding wears the channel deeper.

Water also attacks rock in other ways. Flowing water pries loose fractured blocks and carries them away. Chemical reactions can dissolve certain rocks, such as limestone, and weaken the rest. Each of these processes removes material and lets the river sink lower.

Uplift is what makes a deep canyon possible. When tectonic forces raise the land, the river gains energy because it has farther to fall toward sea level. The river responds by cutting down faster to keep its old course. The Colorado River and the Colorado Plateau show this pairing clearly.

Canyon walls widen through a separate set of forces. Rain, frost, and gravity break down the cliffs and send debris tumbling to the river below. Harder rock layers form steep cliffs, while softer layers erode into slopes. This difference gives many canyons their stepped profile.

Floods speed up the work dramatically. A single large flood can move boulders that normal flows never budge. Much of a canyon's growth may happen during these rare, powerful events.

**Cloud storage** is a service that lets you save files on someone else's computers over the internet instead of (or in addition to) your own device. You access them through an app, website, or a folder that syncs automatically. Examples include Google Drive, Dropbox, iCloud, and OneDrive.

**Where your files actually are**

Your files are stored on servers in **data centers**: large, secure buildings full of computers and hard drives/SSDs, run by the provider (Google, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, etc.) or sometimes rented from another company. A few details:

- **Physical location:** Data centers are located in many countries. Your files may be in a region near you, but providers often choose locations for efficiency, and some let you pick a region (mostly business plans).
- **Copies:** Your files are usually **replicated** across multiple drives, and often multiple data centers, so a hardware failure doesn't lose your data.
- **Fragmentation:** Large files may be split into pieces and stored across different machines, then reassembled when you open them.
- **Your device:** Many services also keep a local synced copy on your computer or phone, so you may have the file in both places. If you use "online-only" or "files on demand" options, the file is only in the cloud until you open it.

**Security basics**

- Files are typically **encrypted** while traveling over the internet and while stored on the provider's servers.
- Most services hold the encryption keys, which means they can technically access your data (for example, to scan for malware or respond to legal requests). A few services offer **end-to-end encryption** (like Proton Drive or Tresorit), where only you hold the keys.
- Use a strong password and two-factor authentication, since your account is the main way someone could get at your files.

**Pros and cons**

- **Pros:** Access from any device, easy sharing, automatic backup, protection from losing a single device.
- **Cons:** Needs internet for most features, ongoing subscription costs for larger amounts of storage, and you depend on the provider's policies and security.

**Tip:** Cloud sync isn't the same as a true backup. If you delete a file or it gets corrupted, the change can sync everywhere. Many people keep an additional backup of important files.

Prime numbers matter in cryptography because multiplying them is easy, but reversing the multiplication is hard.

**The core asymmetry**

Multiplying two large primes takes a computer a fraction of a second. Starting from the product and finding the two original primes takes far longer. For numbers hundreds of digits long, the task is infeasible with current methods.

**How this builds a public-key system**

RSA, a widely used encryption scheme, relies on this asymmetry. Two large primes are chosen and kept secret. Their product is published as part of the public key. Anyone can use the public key to lock a message, but only someone who knows the original primes can unlock it.

**A puzzle box analogy**

Think of a puzzle box that anyone can snap shut, but that opens only if you know its hidden solution. The public key is the box that anyone can close. The primes are the secret solution that opens it. Building the box is simple, but solving it without the secret is impractical.

**Why primes specifically**

Every whole number has exactly one prime factorization. This gives the math a clean and predictable structure. Primes also make it possible to compute certain values, such as Euler's totient, that the private key depends on.

**Other uses**

Primes also appear in Diffie-Hellman key exchange and in elliptic curve systems. Those methods use a different hard problem, the discrete logarithm. They still depend on arithmetic performed with respect to a large prime.

**The main risk**

Quantum computers running Shor's algorithm could factor large numbers efficiently. This threatens RSA and similar systems. Researchers are developing post-quantum cryptography to replace them.

Mars looks red because of iron oxide in its soil and dust. This is the same compound we know as rust.

Iron is common in Martian rocks. Over billions of years, it reacted with oxygen and water. That reaction produced the reddish iron oxide.

Winds then spread the fine dust across the planet. The dust coats the surface and also hangs in the thin atmosphere. This gives the whole planet a rusty orange-red tint when seen from Earth.

The red is not uniform, though. Some regions are darker, with exposed basaltic rock that looks gray or brown. The sky on Mars also looks butterscotch or tan during the day because of the suspended dust.

Scientists find planets around other stars by looking for the small effects those planets have on their host stars. Planets are faint and sit very close to bright stars, so direct viewing is rare. Most discoveries come from indirect clues, and each clue is like a jigsaw piece that helps complete the picture.

The transit method is the most productive technique. A planet passes in front of its star as seen from Earth. The star's light dips slightly during the crossing. Telescopes such as Kepler and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) measure these dips. The depth of the dip reveals the planet's size, and the timing of repeated dips reveals its orbital period.

The radial velocity method tracks the star's motion. A planet's gravity tugs the star back and forth. This motion shifts the star's light slightly toward blue, then toward red. Astronomers detect the shifts by splitting the light into a spectrum. The size of the shift gives the planet's minimum mass.

Direct imaging captures light from the planet itself. It works best for young, giant planets that sit far from their stars. Instruments block the starlight with a device called a coronagraph. The planet then appears as a faint dot nearby.

Gravitational microlensing uses a star's gravity as a magnifying lens. When a star passes in front of a more distant one, the background star brightens. A planet around the nearer star adds a short extra blip to that brightening. This method can find planets that other techniques miss.

Astrometry measures tiny wobbles in a star's position on the sky. The method is difficult, but the European Space Agency's Gaia mission is making it more practical.

Combining methods gives the fullest picture. Transits supply a planet's size, and radial velocity supplies its mass. Together they give its density, which hints at whether the planet is rocky or gaseous. Each method fits with the others like interlocking jigsaw pieces.

A microwave oven heats food with electromagnetic waves. These waves have a frequency of about 2.45 gigahertz.

A part called a magnetron generates the waves. It converts electrical energy into microwaves.

The waves travel into the cooking chamber. Metal walls reflect them, so they bounce around inside.

Food contains water, fats, and sugars. Water molecules are polar, meaning one end is slightly positive and the other slightly negative.

The microwaves create an oscillating electric field. This field makes the polar molecules rotate back and forth billions of times per second.

The rotating molecules bump into their neighbors. This friction turns motion into thermal energy.

That thermal energy is what heats the food. Fats and sugars absorb microwaves too, though less strongly than water.

Microwaves penetrate only about an inch or two into food. The interior then warms by ordinary conduction.

A rotating turntable helps even out the heating. The waves form hot and cold spots, and rotation moves the food through them.

Metal mesh in the door keeps the waves inside. The holes are much smaller than the wavelength, so the waves cannot pass through.

The Silk Road was a network of overland and maritime routes linking China, Central Asia, India, Persia, and the Mediterranean. It operated for roughly 1,500 years.

It moved luxury goods across vast distances. Silk, spices, porcelain, and precious stones traveled west. Gold, silver, glassware, horses, and wool traveled east.

Trade rarely happened in a single journey. Goods passed through many hands, with merchants handing cargo to others at oasis towns and trading hubs like Samarkand, Kashgar, and Palmyra. Each stage added cost, so a product's price rose sharply by the time it reached Europe.

The routes also spread ideas and technologies. Buddhism moved from India into China, and Islam spread across Central Asia. Papermaking and gunpowder traveled west, changing how Europeans recorded information and fought wars.

Disease moved along the same paths. The Black Death likely spread through these networks in the 1300s, with devastating effects across Europe.

The network declined as sea routes opened. After the 1400s, European powers sailed directly to Asia, bypassing the middlemen and the overland costs. This shift moved economic power toward Atlantic trading states.

The Silk Road left a lasting legacy as an early model of global connection, linking distant cultures through commerce.

Most black holes begin as massive stars. A star stays stable because two forces balance each other. Gravity pulls its material inward, while heat and pressure from nuclear fusion push outward.

That balance ends when the star runs out of fuel. A star at least about 20 times the Sun's mass can no longer make enough energy in its core. Fusion stops, and the outward push vanishes. Gravity wins.

The core then collapses in less than a second. Outer layers often rebound and blast into space as a supernova. The core, however, keeps shrinking. If the leftover mass exceeds roughly three times the Sun's, nothing known can halt the collapse.

The collapse creates a region where escape becomes impossible. Think of a cyclist coasting up a hill. A strong push lets the rider crest it, but a steeper hill demands more speed. Squeeze a mass into a small enough space and the "hill" gets so steep that even light can't climb out. The boundary of that region is the event horizon.

Stellar collapse is not the only route. Supermassive black holes, which sit at the centers of galaxies, likely grew by swallowing gas and stars and by merging with other black holes over billions of years. Some astronomers also propose primordial black holes, which would have formed from dense pockets of matter in the early universe. Evidence for those remains unconfirmed.

Cutting an onion breaks open its cells. This mixes chemicals that were stored apart.

One of these is an enzyme called alliinase. It converts sulfur compounds in the onion into sulfenic acid. A second enzyme, lachrymatory factor synthase, then rearranges that acid. The result is a volatile gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide.

The gas drifts up toward your face. It reaches the surface of your eyes and reacts with the water there. This reaction forms a mild sulfur-containing acid, which irritates the nerve endings in your cornea.

Your brain reads this irritation as a threat. It signals the tear glands to flush the eye. The tears wash away the irritant, and that is why you cry.

Several things reduce the effect. Chilling the onion beforehand slows the chemical reactions. A very sharp knife breaks fewer cells than a dull one. Cutting near a fan or under a vent carries the gas away from your eyes. Wearing goggles blocks the gas entirely.

A mortgage calculator uses a standard formula for fixed-rate loans.

**The formula**

M = P × [r(1 + r)^n] / [(1 + r)^n − 1]

**What each part means**

- M is the monthly payment.
- P is the loan amount (principal).
- r is the monthly interest rate.
- n is the total number of monthly payments.

**How you get r and n**

- Divide the annual rate by 12 to get r.
- Multiply the loan term in years by 12 to get n.

**An example**

- Suppose the loan is $300,000 at 6% for 30 years.
- Then r is 0.005, and n is 360.
- The term (1.005)^360 is about 6.0226.
- The payment works out to about $1,798.65 per month.

**Why the formula works**

- It finds the fixed payment that pays off the loan exactly at the end of the term.
- Each month, interest is charged on the remaining balance.
- The rest of the payment reduces the principal.
- Early payments are mostly interest.
- Later payments are mostly principal.

**What calculators often add**

- Property taxes are usually added to the monthly total.
- Homeowners insurance is often included as well.
- Private mortgage insurance may apply if your down payment is small.
- HOA fees are sometimes included too.

**A limit to know**

- The formula assumes a fixed rate.
- Adjustable-rate mortgages need the payment recalculated whenever the rate changes.

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s. No single cause explains this. Historians treat the evidence like a jigsaw puzzle, where several pieces had to be present before the picture appeared.

The first piece is energy. Britain had large coal deposits, often close to rivers, canals, and ports. This made coal cheap to extract and move.

The second piece is the price of labor. British wages were unusually high compared with the cost of energy. Robert Allen argues that this made machines worth the investment, because they replaced expensive workers with cheap coal.

The third piece is agriculture. Farming improvements raised output per worker. This freed people to move into towns and factory work while still keeping them fed.

The fourth piece is institutions. Property rights were relatively secure, and Parliament was responsive to commercial interests. Patents and contract law also gave inventors and investors some confidence that they could keep the rewards.

The fifth piece is trade and capital. Overseas commerce, including the Atlantic trade and colonial markets, supplied raw materials like cotton. It also created demand for manufactured goods and generated wealth that could be invested. Historians disagree about how large this piece is, partly because much of that wealth came from slavery and coercion.

The sixth piece is practical knowledge. Britain had many skilled craftsmen, instrument makers, and mechanics. Scientific societies and a culture of experimentation helped spread ideas. Inventions like the steam engine came from people who could both understand the theory and build the machine.

The seventh piece is geography. Britain is an island with many harbors and navigable rivers. This lowered transport costs and protected the country from the land wars that devastated much of continental Europe.

No one piece is enough on its own. China and the Netherlands had some of these features, but neither had the full combination. Britain was the place where the pieces came together, and that fit produced the shift to mechanized, fossil-fueled production.

Ocean tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun on Earth's oceans.

**The Moon's role**
- The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's water. The side of Earth facing the Moon experiences a stronger pull, creating a bulge of water, a high tide.
- A second bulge forms on the opposite side of Earth. This happens because the Moon pulls less strongly on the far side than on the Earth's center, so the water there is effectively "left behind." Put another way, it's the *difference* in gravitational pull across Earth (the tidal force) that matters.
- As Earth rotates, any given coastline passes through both bulges each day, giving most places two high tides and two low tides roughly every 24 hours and 50 minutes. (The extra 50 minutes comes from the Moon moving along its orbit while Earth spins.)

**The Sun's role**
- The Sun is much more massive but far more distant, so its tidal effect is about 46% as strong as the Moon's.
- When the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up (new and full moon), their effects combine to produce **spring tides**, which are unusually high and low.
- When the Sun and Moon are at right angles (first and third quarter moons), their effects partly cancel, producing **neap tides**, which have a smaller range.

**Other factors that shape local tides**
- Coastline shape, ocean basin size, and seafloor depth can amplify or dampen tides. The Bay of Fundy in Canada, for example, sees ranges over 15 meters.
- Some places, like parts of the Gulf of Mexico, have only one high and one low tide per day.
- Weather, such as storms and air pressure, can raise or lower water levels beyond the predicted tide.
